In 1999 he founded IHOPKC, a round-the-clock prayer ministry with a strong end-times emphasis and international influence. In late 2023 IHOPKC ended its relationship with him following allegations of past sexual misconduct.

positions.context:
The movement draws on the 1948 Latter Rain revival in Saskatchewan, which taught restored apostles and prophets, laying on of hands to impart gifts, and an end-time 'manifested' church. The Assemblies of God rejected it in 1949. The ideas survived in independent networks and resurfaced through the 1970s charismatic renewal. In the late 1980s John Wimber's Vineyard briefly brought the Kansas City Prophets to a wide evangelical audience. In the 1990s Wagner's research on fast-growing independent churches in the Global South and the United States gave the apostolic side a name and an organisational form.

The movement is global and decentralised. Wagner estimated hundreds of millions of adherents worldwide, a figure critics and scholars treat with caution. Prophetic conferences, schools of ministry and media platforms spread its practices well beyond formal networks. After 2016, high-profile prophecies about American politics brought it unusual public attention.
claims: Christ gave apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers 'till we all come' to maturity, so all five remain until the church is complete.
God has restored the offices of prophet (from the 1980s) and apostle (from the 1990s) as part of a progressive restoration of the church.
Apostles exercise governmental authority over networks of churches and ministries, and prophets give revelation to guide them.
Prophets receive revelation for individuals, churches, cities and nations, including predictive words.
New Testament prophecy does not add to Scripture, is partial, and must be weighed. Inaccurate words call for correction, not automatic condemnation as a false prophet.
Strategic-level spiritual warfare against territorial spirits is part of advancing God's kingdom.
The restored apostolic and prophetic ministries prepare the church for end-time harvest and for transforming society.

scriptures.reading: The five gifts are given 'till we all come' to the unity of the faith and a perfect man. Since that goal has not been reached, apostles and prophets continue.
The church is built on the foundation of apostles and prophets. Every generation needs foundation-laying ministry for new churches and nations.
God has set in the church first apostles, secondly prophets. The order describes the church's permanent structure, not a first-century exception.
Prophets and teachers at Antioch heard the Spirit commission Barnabas and Saul. This is a model for prophetic direction of mission.
Agabus predicted a famine, and the church acted on it. Predictive prophecy guides practical decisions.
God does nothing without revealing his secret to his servants the prophets. Prophets are needed to discern what God is doing.
God promised to pour out his Spirit on all flesh so that sons and daughters prophesy, a promise for the whole church age (Acts 2:17-18).
We prophesy in part. New Testament prophecy is real but partial, which explains why prophets can be wrong in details.
Believers wrestle against principalities and powers, which supports strategic warfare against spiritual powers over regions.

arguments.text: Ephesians 4:11-13 ties all five ministries to the same purpose and the same time span, 'till we all come' to maturity. Removing the first two while keeping the other three is arbitrary.

The New Testament names apostles beyond the Twelve and Paul, such as Barnabas, James the Lord's brother, Andronicus and Junia, and possibly Silas and Timothy. So 'apostle' is not limited to eyewitnesses of the resurrection.
Paul commands believers to desire to prophesy and not to forbid it, and to judge prophecies rather than reject them. That presumes ongoing, fallible congregational prophecy.

Prophecy and visions continued after the apostles, in the *Didache*'s instructions on testing travelling prophets, in second-century accounts and in later revival movements. On this view cessation was a later theological assumption, not the church's original experience.
Rapid church growth in independent apostolic networks in Africa, Latin America and Asia, which Wagner documented as a missiologist, is presented as fruit validating the model.
Denominational bureaucracy tends to slow mission. Relational apostolic networks allow quicker, Spirit-led response, as in the book of Acts.

critiques.from: Holly Pivec and R. Douglas Geivett
critiques.text: The movement claims for its apostles and prophets a governmental authority and revelatory role that the New Testament gives only to the foundational apostles and prophets. In practice this places followers under leaders whose words function like extra-biblical revelation.

Deuteronomy 18 requires that a prophet who speaks presumptuously in God's name must not be heeded. The movement's record of failed predictions, especially about the 2020 US election, exposes the gift as counterfeit.

critiques.from: Ernie Gruen and other charismatic critics (1990)
critiques.text: Gruen, a Kansas City pastor, documented what he saw as manipulative prophecy, elitism and doctrinal error at Kansas City Fellowship. Later moral failures involving leading prophets confirmed fears about character and accountability.

critiques.from: Assemblies of God position paper 'Apostles and Prophets' (2001)
critiques.text: Classical Pentecostals welcomed apostolic and prophetic ministry functions but warned against self-appointed offices claiming authority over churches and against restoring Latter Rain errors that the denomination had rejected in 1949.

critiques.from: Journalists and scholars of religion and politics
critiques.text: Politicised prophecy, such as declaring election outcomes and casting political opponents as demonic, has damaged the credibility of the prophetic gift and contributed to unrest after the 2020 election.

responses.text: Wagner and others answered that today's apostles do not write Scripture and are not equal to the Twelve. Their authority is relational and functional, and it is accepted voluntarily by those who align with them.

Proponents argue that Deuteronomy 18 governed Old Testament canonical prophets. New Testament prophecy is 'in part' and is to be weighed, so a mistaken word calls for correction and repentance, not stoning or automatic dismissal.

Leaders including John Wimber and Mike Bickle acknowledged errors in the early Kansas City period and introduced correction. Defenders argue that the sins of individuals do not invalidate a biblical gift.
Many apostolic leaders agree with warnings against self-appointment and point to their own accountability structures, such as apostolic councils, alignment and mutual submission.

Some prophets apologised publicly for 2020 election words, and many leaders now caution against partisan prophecy. Defenders add that political prophecies are a small fraction of prophetic ministry, most of which concerns individuals and local churches.

strawMen.strawMan: NAR prophets claim their words are equal to Scripture.
strawMen.correction: Most proponents explicitly say prophecy today is subordinate to Scripture and must be tested by it. Critics' concern is that in practice prophetic words can function with near-scriptural authority.

strawMen.strawMan: The NAR is a single organisation with a membership list.
strawMen.correction: It is a loose web of networks, ministries and teachings. Many leaders who share its practices reject the label, which is why both proponents and careful critics describe it as a movement, not a denomination.

strawMen.strawMan: Everyone who believes in prophecy today belongs to the NAR.
strawMen.correction: Most continuationists, including many Pentecostal denominations, practise prophecy without accepting apostolic offices with governmental authority. Some are strong critics of the NAR.

positive: Renewed expectancy for the Spirit's gifts and for hearing God among many believers.
Fuelled extensive prayer movements, such as 24-hour prayer rooms, and missionary energy.
Supported fast-growing independent churches in the Global South with flexible leadership structures.
negative: Failed predictions, especially in 2020, damaged public trust in prophecy.
Leader-centred networks with weak accountability have been linked to several moral and spiritual-abuse scandals.
Fusion of prophecy with partisan politics divided churches.
Some followers have made life decisions on prophetic words that later proved mistaken.

positions.name: Critics of the apostolic-prophetic movement
positions.summary:
Critics argue that the movement misreads the New Testament on apostles and prophets, and so creates a class of leaders who claim revelatory authority that Scripture does not give. They come from two camps.

Cessationists such as John MacArthur hold that revelatory gifts ended with the apostolic age and the closing of the canon. Continuationist and non-committal evangelicals such as Holly Pivec and R. Douglas Geivett, who deliberately do not rest their case on cessationism, argue that even if spiritual gifts continue, the NAR's particular claims are unbiblical: governing apostles, prophets who direct nations, strategic-level spiritual warfare and new revelation for the church's mission.

Both camps stress the biblical tests of prophecy, the sufficiency of Scripture, the accountability of leaders, and the documented record of failed predictions and moral scandals.

His 2013 Strange Fire conference and book argued that modern prophecy, tongues and healing are not the biblical gifts and that the movement as a whole is spiritually dangerous. His broad brush drew criticism from continuationist evangelicals.

figures.profession: Charismatic pastor, Full Faith Church of Love, Kansas City

figures.profession: New Testament scholar, Southern Baptist Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Schreiner had earlier been open to continuing prophecy. In a 2018 book he argued that New Testament prophecy was infallible revelation and that, since the foundation of apostles and prophets has been laid, the gift has ceased. He made the case with notable charity toward continuationists.

works.author: Thomas R. Schreiner
works.title: Spiritual Gifts: What They Are and Why They Matter

positions.context:
Criticism started inside the charismatic world, with Gruen's 1990 report on Kansas City and with classical Pentecostal concern about the revival of Latter Rain ideas, which led to the Assemblies of God's 2001 paper on apostles and prophets. Wagner's use of the 'NAR' label made the movement easier to analyse. In 2011 a radio interview and press coverage linking the NAR to political 'dominionism' prompted Wagner to publish a response defending the movement and denying theocratic aims.

After 2016, and especially after the failed 2020 election prophecies and 6 January 2021, criticism from evangelicals, ex-members and journalists grew sharply. Former participants added testimony about spiritual abuse.
claims: The apostles of Ephesians 2:20 were a unique foundational group, eyewitnesses commissioned by the risen Christ, and that foundation has been laid once for all.
Scripture is sufficient and the faith has been once delivered. No present-day leader can claim revelatory authority to direct the church.
Biblical tests of prophecy include accuracy (Deuteronomy 18), orthodoxy (Deuteronomy 13; 1 John 4) and character (Matthew 7). Many modern prophets fail them.
Governing apostolic offices outside accountable church structures foster authoritarianism and spiritual abuse.
Practices such as strategic-level spiritual warfare and spiritual mapping lack biblical warrant.
Political prophecy has harmed the church's witness and treated partisan causes as the will of God.

scriptures.reading: A prophet whose prediction in the Lord's name does not come to pass has spoken presumptuously and is not to be feared.
Even a prophet whose sign comes true is false if he leads people after other gods. Accuracy alone is not enough.
The apostles and prophets are the foundation, with Christ the cornerstone. A foundation is laid once and then built upon.
An apostle in the full sense had to be a witness of Jesus' ministry and resurrection.
Paul calls himself the last to whom the risen Christ appeared, 'as of one born out of due time'. The line of resurrection witnesses closes with him.
God has spoken finally in his Son in these last days. The era of new revelation culminates in Christ and the apostolic witness.
The faith was once for all delivered to the saints, not progressively revealed through new prophets.
False prophets are known by their fruits. Character and outcomes matter.
Prophets who speak a vision of their own heart, not from the Lord's mouth, are not to be heeded.
Paul warns of 'false apostles' and 'super-apostles' who transform themselves into apostles of Christ.

arguments.text: Ephesians 2:20 makes apostles and prophets the church's foundation. Ephesians 3:5 says the mystery was revealed to them. Their role was to lay down revelation, so it is unrepeatable, just as a building gets one foundation.

Apostleship in the governing sense required having seen the risen Lord and being personally commissioned, and Paul presents himself as the last such witness. The wider 'apostles' (Barnabas and others) were missionary envoys of churches, not governing officers over networks.
Deuteronomy 18 gives a clear accuracy test that the New Testament never revokes. Prophecies about specific outcomes, such as elections, pandemics and dates, that do not happen fall under it.

The movement's own history includes repeated failed predictions and moral collapses among celebrated prophets. Examples include the Kansas City controversies of 1990, the Lakeland revival of 2008 and its aftermath, and many 2020 election prophecies. Critics read this as a pattern, not as isolated lapses.

The Assemblies of God rejected the 1948 Latter Rain movement's restoration of apostles and prophets in 1949, and reaffirmed caution in 2001. Classical Pentecostals have therefore long seen the NAR's distinctive claims as an aberration.

If apostles have governing authority and prophets speak for God, followers have no practical way to dissent without seeming to resist God. That structure invites abuse regardless of any leader's intentions.

critiques.text: Critics create a monolithic 'NAR' that does not exist, attribute fringe statements to everyone, and quote selectively from leaders who reject the label.

critiques.from: Continuationist scholars (e.g. Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms)
critiques.text: Applying Deuteronomy 18's death-penalty standard to New Testament congregational prophecy ignores Paul's instruction to weigh prophecies, which presupposes that some will be partly wrong.

critiques.from: Continuationist critics of cessationism (e.g. Michael Brown, *Authentic Fire*)
critiques.text: Cessationist critics like MacArthur condemn the whole charismatic movement, hundreds of millions of believers, on the basis of its worst examples. That is unfair and unbiblical.
Western critics may misread apostolic leadership in contexts where informal, charismatic leadership is the normal and effective form of church growth.

responses.text: Pivec and Geivett distinguish a 'formal' NAR, meaning leaders who adopt the offices and teachings explicitly, from a wider 'informal' influence, and they document views from leaders' own writings. Wagner himself coined and used the label.

Critics such as Schreiner argue that Agabus's prophecy in Acts 21 was substantially accurate. On this reading 'weighing' prophecy means judging whether it is from God, not sorting true parts from false parts of a genuine prophecy.

Non-cessationist critics such as Pivec and Geivett explicitly avoid blanket condemnation and focus on specific teachings. Even some cessationists acknowledge that individual charismatics may be sincere believers.

Critics respond that the issue is not leadership style but claims of revelatory authority. They note that African and Latin American theologians have themselves criticised abuses by self-styled apostles and prophets.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics of the NAR are all cessationists who deny the Spirit's gifts.
strawMen.correction: Several prominent critics, including classical Pentecostals and continuationist evangelicals, affirm present-day gifts and object specifically to governing apostles and directive prophets.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics think every prophetic word is demonic.
strawMen.correction: Most critics attribute failed prophecies to human imagination, presumption or misunderstanding, as in Jeremiah 23:16, rather than to demonic deception. Some cessationists do warn of spiritual deception.

positive: Gave pastors and families vocabulary and resources to evaluate teachings entering their churches.
Pressed for accountability and documented patterns of failed prophecy and abuse.
Contributed to internal reforms within the charismatic world.
negative: Broad cessationist polemic has alienated many sincere charismatics and hardened divisions.
The 'NAR' label is sometimes applied loosely to any charismatic church.
Debates have sometimes become personal rather than exegetical.

adherents: Cessationist Reformed and Baptist evangelicals
Many classical Pentecostal leaders cautious of Latter Rain ideas
Continuationist evangelicals critical of NAR distinctives
Former participants in apostolic-prophetic networks

positions.name: Continuationist reformers: prophecy with accountability
positions.summary:
A third group believes that prophecy and other spiritual gifts continue today, but insists that they be practised under clear biblical guardrails. Following Wayne Grudem's influential argument, it treats ordinary New Testament prophecy as a human report of something God brings to mind. Such prophecy is fallible and lacks the authority of Scripture, and it must be weighed by the church.

The reformers often favour a 'functional' view of apostles, meaning pioneering church planters and missionaries, over a governing office equal to the Twelve. They call prophets to public accountability for failed words, warn against partisan and date-setting prophecy, and insist that character counts for more than gifting. After the failed 2020 election prophecies, voices such as Michael Brown called for repentance and helped promote the Prophetic Standards statement. Earlier, J. Lee Grady and Sam Storms had written practical correctives.

figures.name: Wayne Grudem
figures.profession: Systematic theologian, Phoenix Seminary
figures.bio: Grudem is a Reformed Baptist continuationist. His 1988 book argued that New Testament congregational prophecy differs from Old Testament and apostolic revelation: it is fallible and must be evaluated, and it does not threaten the sufficiency of Scripture. This 'two-tier' view gave many evangelicals a framework for openness to prophecy with guardrails.

figures.name: John Wimber
figures.profession: Founding leader of the Association of Vineyard Churches
figures.bio: Wimber brought the Kansas City Prophets into the Vineyard in 1990 and tried to correct their practice with stronger pastoral oversight and biblical teaching. Later in the 1990s he distanced the Vineyard from some prophetic emphases. His approach, openness with accountability, became a model for later reformers.

positions.context:
Reform efforts have come in waves after crises. Wimber's oversight of the Kansas City Prophets followed the 1990 Gruen controversy. Critiques followed the Lakeland revival in 2008. The largest wave followed 2020, when numerous well-known prophets had confidently predicted Donald Trump's re-election. Some, such as Jeremiah Johnson in January 2021, publicly apologised and reported receiving harsh backlash from followers. Others reinterpreted their words or kept to them.

The Prophetic Standards statement followed in 2021. It was drafted by charismatic leaders and called for accountability, humility, correction of failed words and avoidance of manipulation. Supporters see it as a sign the movement can police itself. Sceptics note that it has no enforcement mechanism.
claims: Prophecy continues as a gift for the church's edification, exhortation and comfort, and believers should earnestly desire it.
Ordinary New Testament prophecy is fallible human speech prompted by revelation. It never equals Scripture and must be weighed.
'Apostle' today is best understood functionally (church planter, missionary, pioneer), not as a governing office equal to the Twelve.
Prophets must publicly acknowledge and correct failed words, and churches should hold them accountable.
Prophetic ministry should avoid partisan politics, date-setting, control and financial manipulation.
Character, fruit and orthodoxy are essential tests alongside accuracy.

scriptures.reading: Prophecy speaks to people for edification, exhortation and comfort. Its normal purpose is upbuilding, not direction of nations.
Let two or three prophets speak and the others weigh what is said. Prophecy is subject to communal evaluation.
Do not despise prophecies, but test everything. This rules out both blanket rejection and naive acceptance.
Test the spirits, because many false prophets have gone out. Testing is a standing duty.
Presumptuous prediction is serious. Even if New Testament prophecy is not under the death penalty, prophets who miss must own it and not be trusted blindly.
Agabus's prophecy was broadly true but arguably inexact in detail (compare 21:33). Grudem uses it as an example of fallible New Testament prophecy.
Prophetic power without love is nothing. Character matters more than gift.
Some who prophesied in Jesus' name will be disowned. Gifting is no proof of approval.

arguments.text: Paul treats prophecy as something to be weighed and partly sifted. That implies congregational prophecy could include error without the speaker being a false prophet, which distinguishes it from canonical prophecy.
Paul tells the church to desire prophecy and not to forbid tongues, so wholesale cessation contradicts apostolic instruction. Paul is equally clear that 'all things be done decently and in order'.

The *Didache* (late first or early second century) both welcomed travelling prophets and gave practical tests: a prophet who asked for money or overstayed was false. Reformers see this as the earliest model of accountable prophecy.
Failed prophecies in 2020 and the subsequent apologies show the need for formal standards. Without accountability, the gift's credibility collapses.
Treating prophecy as fallible protects the sufficiency of Scripture and lets the church practise the gift without making every word binding.

critiques.from: Cessationist scholars (e.g. Richard Gaffin, Thomas Schreiner)
critiques.text: 'Fallible prophecy' is a category the Bible does not know. In Scripture, prophecy is God's word; if a word can be wrong, it is not prophecy. Agabus's prophecy was not erroneous.
Reformers can quench the Spirit and create a culture of fear around prophetic ministry. Public 'calling out' of prophets violates honour and should be handled privately.

critiques.from: Critics such as Pivec and Geivett
critiques.text: Standards statements lack enforcement. Many prophets whose 2020 words failed continued their ministries with large followings and without public retraction.
Similar reform moments in 1990 and 2008 did not prevent later crises. Without structural change, reform statements may be cyclical damage control.

responses.text: Grudem and others reply that Paul's instruction to weigh prophecies and not 'despise' them would make no sense if every genuine prophecy were infallible. They also argue that the Greek usage of 'prophet' in the New Testament era was broader than canonical prophecy.
Reformers answer that the same verse that says 'quench not the Spirit' goes on to say 'prove all things'. Public prophecies, especially about nations, require public correction.

Reformers acknowledge the enforcement gap. They argue that the remedy lies in local church accountability and in congregants choosing whom to follow, not in a central authority, which their ecclesiology lacks.
They accept the historical point and argue that each crisis has nonetheless produced growing consensus around Scripture's primacy, prophetic humility and pastoral oversight.

strawMen.strawMan: Reformers are cessationists in disguise.
strawMen.correction: They practise and encourage prophecy and other gifts. Their concern is how prophecy is practised, not whether it exists.

strawMen.strawMan: Fallible prophecy means prophets can say anything without consequence.
strawMen.correction: Reformers argue the opposite. Because prophecy is fallible it must be tested, and repeated failure should disqualify someone from public prophetic ministry.

positive: Gave continuationist churches a framework to practise prophecy without undermining Scripture.
Produced public apologies and clearer ethical standards after 2020.
Modelled self-critique within the charismatic movement.
negative: Reform statements have had limited reach among high-profile independent prophets.
The 'fallible prophecy' concept is contested and, critics say, may lower the stakes of speaking in God's name.

Pentecostal and charismatic scholars and pastors seeking accountability
Evangelical continuationists influenced by Grudem
Signatories and supporters of the Prophetic Standards statement

readings.reading: All five gifts, including apostles and prophets, last 'till we all come' to maturity, so the offices continue today.
The gifts serve maturity, but Ephesians 2:20 shows the apostles and prophets as the once-laid foundation. Their continuing function is through their recorded teaching.
The functions continue: pioneering apostolic work and prophetic encouragement. A governing office equal to the Twelve does not.
Every new church and nation needs foundation-laying apostolic and prophetic ministry.
A foundation is laid once. The apostles and prophets of the first century gave the church its revealed basis.
The foundational apostles and prophets are unique. Present prophecy builds on that foundation and never adds to it.
This applied to Old Testament covenant prophets. New Testament prophecy is 'in part', and mistakes call for correction.
A permanent test. Prophets whose specific predictions fail have spoken presumptuously and should not be heeded.
The death penalty does not carry over, but the principle does: failed predictions must be owned, and repeated failure disqualifies.
Prophecy is weighed, normally by other mature prophets and leaders.
The church judges whether a message is from God at all. Weighing does not mean accepting a mixture of truth and error as genuine prophecy.
The whole congregation weighs prophecy, which shows it is fallible and subordinate to Scripture.
Do not despise prophecy. Critics who reject it wholesale disobey this command.
'Prove all things.' Testing is mandatory, and much modern prophecy fails the test.
Both halves matter: neither despise nor accept uncritically.
Agabus models New Testament predictive prophecy that guides the church.
Agabus's prophecy was accurate in substance. It is an example of reliable prophecy, not fallible prophecy.
On Grudem's reading, Agabus was right in substance but inexact in detail (the Romans, not the Jews, bound Paul), which shows New Testament prophecy is fallible.
God's final word is Christ. Present prophecy points to him and adds no new doctrine.
With the Son's coming, revelation reaches its climax. Claims to ongoing directive revelation undermine this finality.
Christ is God's final word. Prophecy today applies, never adds to, that revelation.

title: Divine healing: from the early church to Bethel
question: Should Christians expect God to heal the sick miraculously today, is healing guaranteed to faith, and how should claims of healing be evaluated?
intro:
Prayer for the sick is as old as the church. James instructs elders to anoint and pray for the sick, and early Christian writers such as Irenaeus and Augustine reported healings in their own day. In the modern period a distinct divine-healing movement took shape. It began with Johann Christoph Blumhardt in Germany and the nineteenth-century 'faith-cure' movement (Charles Cullis, A. J. Gordon, A. B. Simpson). It continued through Pentecostal healers such as Smith Wigglesworth and John G. Lake, the post-war healing revivals and Kathryn Kuhlman, then John Wimber's 'power evangelism' and today's Bethel Church in Redding, California.

The debate has three main positions. Healing-movement teachers hold that healing is provided in the atonement and that God's will is to heal. Mediating 'kingdom' continuationists, shaped by George Ladd's 'already and not yet', pray expectantly but deny that healing is guaranteed. Critics include cessationists such as B. B. Warfield, medical sceptics, apologists such as Hank Hanegraaff, and writers on suffering such as Joni Eareckson Tada. They question the claims, the theology, or both.

Since 2010 the debate has also become empirical. Craig Keener's two-volume *Miracles* (2011) gathered thousands of modern claims, and Candy Gunther Brown's *Testing Prayer* (2012) reported field studies of healing prayer. Randomised trials of distant intercessory prayer have found no effect, and documented frauds and child deaths in faith-healing sects give critics evidence of their own.

positions.name: Healing movement: healing in the atonement
positions.summary:
The healing movement holds that Christ's atoning death purchased healing for the body as well as forgiveness for the soul. On this view, as Jesus healed all who came to him, God's will is to heal today, and the church has been commissioned to heal the sick as part of preaching the kingdom.

Sickness is treated as part of the devil's oppression and the curse that Christ came to undo. Faith, both the sick person's and the minister's, is the ordinary channel through which healing comes, and unbelief can hinder it. Different teachers have held this view with different emphases: Blumhardt's pastoral 'Jesus is Victor', Simpson's holiness-shaped 'Christ our Healer', Wigglesworth's bold faith and Bethel's 'Jesus is perfect theology', which holds that the Father's will is seen in Jesus, who never refused to heal anyone.

figures.name: Johann Christoph Blumhardt
figures.profession: Lutheran pastor in Möttlingen and later at Bad Boll, Württemberg
figures.bio: Between 1842 and 1843 Blumhardt engaged in a long pastoral struggle for Gottliebin Dittus, a young woman in his parish he believed was demonically afflicted. It ended, by his account, with the cry 'Jesus is Victor'. A local awakening with confessions and healings followed. He later ran a retreat centre at Bad Boll. His reports, written for church authorities, deeply influenced European and later American healing ministry, and his son Christoph Friedrich and Karl Barth both drew on his legacy.

works.author: Johann Christoph Blumhardt
works.title: Report on Gottliebin Dittus's illness (Krankheitsgeschichte der Gottliebin Dittus)

figures.name: A. B. Simpson
figures.profession: Presbyterian minister, founder of the Christian and Missionary Alliance
figures.bio: Albert Benjamin Simpson suffered from heart trouble and nervous exhaustion. He reported being healed in 1881 after accepting Christ as his healer. He left Presbyterian ministry to found what became the Christian and Missionary Alliance, whose 'fourfold gospel' presents Christ as Saviour, Sanctifier, Healer and Coming King. He taught healing in the atonement and operated healing homes.

figures.name: Smith Wigglesworth
figures.profession: Plumber turned Pentecostal evangelist, Bradford, England
figures.bio: Wigglesworth was barely literate and worked as a plumber before entering itinerant healing ministry after his Pentecostal experience in 1907. He became famous worldwide for bold faith, blunt speech and dramatic healing methods. Reports of healings and even raisings from the dead circulated widely, mostly through admirers' accounts that are hard to verify.

figures.name: John G. Lake
figures.profession: Pentecostal missionary and healing minister
figures.bio: After ministry in South Africa (1908-1913), where he helped found the Apostolic Faith Mission, Lake set up 'healing rooms' in Spokane, Washington, from 1915. Very large numbers of healings were claimed there. Historians note that these figures came from his own reports and that his biography includes embellished claims, but his healing-rooms model was revived in Spokane in 1999 and later spread internationally.

works.title: John G. Lake: Apostle to Africa

figures.name: Bill Johnson
figures.profession: Senior leader of Bethel Church, Redding, California
figures.bio: Under Johnson, Bethel became a global centre for healing and miracle ministry through its School of Supernatural Ministry, music and conferences. He teaches that Jesus is 'perfect theology': since Jesus healed all who came, believers should not build a theology around unanswered prayer. He has also acknowledged publicly that many people they pray for are not healed, including people close to him.

works.title: God Is Good: He's Better Than You Think

positions.context:
The modern movement began in the 1840s-1880s. Pietist awakening in Germany (Blumhardt), Swiss healing homes (Dorothea Trudel), and American holiness and Higher Life piety came together in the faith-cure movement. Its leaders read healing as part of 'full salvation'. Many faith-cure leaders discouraged or relativised medicine, which in that era was often ineffective or harmful.

Pentecostalism after 1906 made healing central to evangelism. The 1947-1958 healing revivals (William Branham, Oral Roberts, A. A. Allen and others) brought tent crusades and radio. Kathryn Kuhlman's meetings, the charismatic renewal and Wimber's Vineyard brought healing prayer into mainline and evangelical churches. Today healing is one of the main reasons people give for converting to Pentecostal Christianity in Africa, Latin America and Asia, and Bethel's model spreads globally through music and training schools.
claims: Christ's atonement provides healing for the body as well as forgiveness of sins.
God's will is revealed in Jesus, who healed all who came to him, so God's will is to heal.
Sickness is part of the devil's oppression and the curse that Christ came to destroy.
Christ commissioned his followers to heal the sick, and that commission continues.
Faith is the normal channel of healing, and unbelief can hinder it.
Healing confirms the gospel and draws people to Christ.
Believers should not let unanswered prayers lower their expectation of what God has promised.

scriptures.reading: The servant bore our griefs (literally 'sicknesses') and carried our sorrows ('pains'). By his stripes we are healed. Physical healing is in the atonement.
Jesus healed all the sick 'that it might be fulfilled' which Isaiah spoke. Matthew himself applies Isaiah 53 to bodily healing.
Jesus healed all who were oppressed of the devil. Sickness is linked to satanic oppression.
The disciples were sent to preach the kingdom and heal the sick, a commission that continues with the church.
The prayer of faith shall save the sick, and the Lord shall raise him up. It is a standing promise to the church.
Believers will lay hands on the sick and they will recover.
'I am the Lord that healeth thee.' Healing is part of God's covenant name and character.
The Lord forgives all iniquities and heals all diseases. Forgiveness and healing go together.
Jesus could do few mighty works in Nazareth because of unbelief. Faith matters for healing.
Those who believe will do the works Jesus did, and greater works.

arguments.text: Matthew 8:17 is decisive. The evangelist applies Isaiah 53:4 to Jesus' healing of physical illness, so the servant's work includes bodily healing.
James gives a standing church practice, with elders, oil and the prayer of faith, and attaches a promise to it. Nothing in the text limits it to the apostolic era.
Jesus is the exact representation of the Father. In the Gospels he never told a sick person that sickness was God's will for them, so believers should not assume it is.

Early Christian writers reported healings well after the apostles. Irenaeus, for example, describes Christians healing the sick by laying on hands. Augustine catalogues healings in North Africa and retracted his earlier view that such miracles had ceased.

Modern revivals from Möttlingen onward have consistently included reports of healing. In global surveys, healing is among the most commonly cited reasons for conversion to Pentecostalism, which is evidence of real effects in many lives.
Lowering expectation to match experience makes experience the norm instead of Scripture. Unanswered prayers should drive believers to press in, not to rewrite God's promises.

critiques.text: Miraculous gifts were credentials of the apostles and accompanied new revelation. They ceased with the apostolic age, and modern faith-cure claims, Protestant or Catholic, rest on misread texts and unreliable testimony.

critiques.from: Medical investigators (William Nolen, 1974) and sceptics (James Randi)
critiques.text: Nolen followed up people reported healed at a Kathryn Kuhlman meeting and found no case of verified cure of organic disease. Randi showed in 1986 that Peter Popoff received information through a hidden earpiece. Claims are often psychosomatic, temporary or fraudulent.
Teaching that healing is guaranteed in the atonement leads inevitably to blaming the sick for weak faith and encourages some to refuse medicine.

critiques.from: Joni Eareckson Tada and theologians of suffering
critiques.text: God sometimes sovereignly withholds physical healing to accomplish deeper purposes. Treating disability or illness as defeat misreads Scripture and isolates suffering believers.

A study of 172 child deaths in faith-healing families in the United States (1975-1995) concluded that most of the children would probably have survived with medical care. Overclaiming has real, measurable costs.

responses.text: Defenders reply that 1 Corinthians 12 presents healing as a gift distributed across the church, not just an apostolic sign. They note that Warfield's cessationism depended partly on Enlightenment criteria for testimony that historians such as Keener now challenge.

Frauds are acknowledged and condemned, but counterfeit currency implies a genuine one. Many healing ministries now encourage medical verification, and Keener and others have collected medically documented cases.

Responsible teachers deny that every unhealed person lacks faith. Bethel and others say plainly that they do not know why some are not healed and that blaming the sick is wrong, while still affirming that God's will revealed in Jesus is to heal.
Healing-movement leaders affirm God's grace in suffering but distinguish persecution, which Christians are promised, from sickness, which Jesus consistently treated as an enemy.
Most healing-movement churches today are not medicine-refusing sects and explicitly endorse medical treatment. The deaths documented came largely from specific isolationist groups.

strawMen.strawMan: Healing teachers claim everyone they pray for is healed.
strawMen.correction: Leaders from Simpson to Bill Johnson have acknowledged that many are not healed. They differ from critics on how to interpret this, not on whether it happens.

strawMen.strawMan: Believing in divine healing means rejecting doctors.
strawMen.correction: Some early faith-cure leaders and some sects discouraged medicine. Most Pentecostal and charismatic churches today combine prayer with medical care.

strawMen.strawMan: The healing movement is a twentieth-century American invention.
strawMen.correction: Its modern form has nineteenth-century German, Swiss and British as well as American roots, and its practice of prayer and anointing draws on James 5 and early church testimony.

positive: Restored prayer for the sick as a normal congregational practice in many churches.
Brought hope and reported healing to very large numbers, especially in places with little medical care.
Drove the growth of Pentecostal and charismatic Christianity worldwide.
negative: Guilt and spiritual trauma among people who were not healed and were told their faith was lacking.
Exploitation by fraudulent healers.
Preventable deaths where medical care was refused, especially of children in isolationist groups.
Credibility damaged by unverified and exaggerated claims.

adherents: Christian and Missionary Alliance (historically, in its 'Christ our Healer' teaching)
Classical Pentecostal denominations, such as the Assemblies of God, which list divine healing as a fundamental truth
Bethel Church and its global network of schools and churches
Healing Rooms ministries and many independent charismatic churches

positions.name: Kingdom continuationists: expectant prayer without guarantee
positions.summary:
This mediating view follows George Eldon Ladd's theology of the kingdom. The kingdom of God has broken into history in Jesus ('already') but is not yet consummated ('not yet'). Healings are real signs of the kingdom's presence, so the church should pray for the sick boldly and regularly, and all believers, not just celebrity healers, may do so.

Complete bodily redemption awaits the resurrection, so healing is not guaranteed in this life, and its absence is not necessarily a sign of weak faith. John Wimber, who taught 'power healing' and himself suffered from cancer and heart disease before he died in 1997, is the defining figure. Kathryn Kuhlman emphasised the sovereign work of the Holy Spirit and refused to explain why some were not healed. The Catholic charismatic Francis MacNutt approached healing as compassionate pastoral prayer. Craig Keener's scholarship argues that miracle claims deserve serious historical investigation.

figures.name: George Eldon Ladd
figures.profession: New Testament scholar, Fuller Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Ladd's work on the kingdom of God as 'already and not yet' became the standard evangelical framework for inaugurated eschatology. Ladd himself was not a healing practitioner, but Wimber built his theology of healing on Ladd's framework.

figures.name: John Wimber
figures.profession: Founding leader of the Association of Vineyard Churches
figures.bio: Wimber was a former rock musician and Quaker-influenced evangelical. While teaching at Fuller Seminary he co-led a famous course on 'Signs, Wonders and Church Growth' (MC510, from 1982). He taught that every believer can pray for the sick in a calm, non-hyped 'naturally supernatural' way. He was candid about the many who were not healed and about his own illnesses.

figures.name: Kathryn Kuhlman
figures.profession: Evangelist, healing minister based in Pittsburgh
figures.bio: From her Pittsburgh meetings beginning in 1948, and through television, Kuhlman drew huge crowds and reported many healings, often announced from the platform as happening in the audience. She insisted she was not a healer and that she did not know why some were healed and others not, attributing everything to the Holy Spirit's sovereignty. Her meetings were also the subject of William Nolen's sceptical investigation.

figures.name: Francis MacNutt
figures.profession: Catholic priest (later laicised), co-founder of Christian Healing Ministries
figures.bio: MacNutt was a leading figure in the Catholic charismatic renewal. His book *Healing* (1974) presented healing prayer as an ordinary expression of Christ's compassion. It emphasised 'soaking prayer', inner healing and healing that is often gradual and partial, and it rejected the idea that the unhealed lack faith.

figures.name: Craig S. Keener
figures.profession: New Testament scholar, Asbury Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Keener's two-volume *Miracles* (2011) argued against David Hume's dismissal of miracle testimony and collected hundreds of modern miracle claims from many countries. Some include medical documentation, among them cases from his own wife's family in Congo. He presents the evidence to show that eyewitness miracle claims are common and cannot be dismissed a priori, not to prove that any particular healing was miraculous.

works.author: Craig S. Keener
works.title: Miracles: The Credibility of the New Testament Accounts

works.author: Craig S. Keener
works.title: Miracles Today: The Supernatural Work of God in the Modern World

positions.context:
The 'kingdom' approach emerged when charismatic renewal reached evangelical and Catholic churches in the 1960s-1980s. Many there wanted healing prayer without the Word of Faith framework or the showmanship of the tent revivals. Wimber's Fuller course and Vineyard conferences, including in the UK, spread a low-key model of 'doing the stuff' in which ordinary members pray for the sick.

Since 2010 a scholarly wing has added empirical and historical study. Keener's *Miracles* (2011) and Candy Gunther Brown's *Testing Prayer* (2012) are central. Brown, a religious-studies scholar, led a study of 'proximal intercessory prayer' in rural Mozambique, published in 2010, which reported measurable improvements in hearing and vision after prayer. She reported her findings cautiously as calling for further research, and they remain debated.
claims: The kingdom of God has broken into the present age, and healings are genuine signs of its presence.
All believers, not only specially gifted healers, may pray for the sick, and they should do so regularly and expectantly.
Full bodily redemption awaits the resurrection, so healing is not guaranteed in this life.
When healing does not come, the sick person should not be blamed. God is sovereign, and the reasons are often hidden.
Medical care is a good gift of God and fully compatible with prayer.
Miracle claims can and should be investigated. Some are well documented and cannot be dismissed a priori.

scriptures.reading: If Jesus casts out demons by the Spirit, the kingdom has come. Healings and deliverance show the kingdom is present now.
Believers who have the Spirit's firstfruits still groan, waiting for the redemption of the body. Full healing is future.
The outward man perishes while the inward man is renewed. Bodies still decline in this age.
Elders and believers pray for one another so that they may be healed. Healing prayer is an ordinary practice of the church.
'Gifts of healings' (plural in Greek) are distributed by the Spirit as he wills, not on demand.
Epaphroditus was sick nearly to death and God had mercy on him. Healing came as mercy, not as an apostolic guarantee.
Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus. Healing was not automatic even in the apostolic circle.
Jesus' mission included recovering of sight to the blind, which is part of the kingdom's good news now.

arguments.text: The New Testament holds together real present healings and continuing sickness among faithful believers, such as Epaphroditus, Trophimus and Timothy. Only an 'already and not yet' framework accounts for both.
Romans 8:23 places the body's redemption in the future. Healings now are foretastes, not the full inheritance.

Keener documents miracle claims across cultures and centuries, many from credible eyewitnesses and some with medical records. Hume's argument that testimony can never establish a miracle assumes what it sets out to prove.

The 2010 Mozambique study led by Candy Gunther Brown reported statistically significant improvements in hearing and vision immediately after hands-on prayer. Brown notes that such effects call for further investigation and do not prove supernatural causation.
If healing were guaranteed, Wimber's own cancer and death, and the deaths of every faithful healer, would be inexplicable. The mediating view fits both Scripture and experience.

Augustine first said miracles were no longer granted, then in *City of God* 22.8 recorded many healings he had witnessed or investigated, while never claiming they were automatic. This is an early model of expectant but sober belief.

critiques.text: 'Already and not yet' can become a theology of disappointment, lowering faith and expectation to match the church's poor experience instead of Jesus' example.

The mediating view still relies largely on anecdote. Keener's cases are mostly unverified testimonies, and if healing is unpredictable and often absent, it is unclear how it differs from ordinary providence.

Large randomised trials such as the 2006 STEP study found no benefit from distant intercessory prayer. Patients who knew they were being prayed for had slightly more complications. Small uncontrolled field studies like Brown's are vulnerable to suggestion, expectancy and measurement bias.

critiques.from: Disability theologians and some evangelical critics
critiques.text: Even gentle expectant prayer in public can objectify disabled people as 'targets' for healing and imply that their bodies are problems to fix.

responses.text: Wimber and others answer that honesty about unanswered prayer protects people from guilt and keeps them praying long-term. They argue that 'not yet' is part of apostolic teaching, not an invention of disappointed charismatics.
Keener replies that testimony is how historians know most of the past, and that his collection includes medically documented cases. A miracle can be both providential and extraordinary.

Defenders reply that distant prayer by strangers in a hospital trial is not the practice the New Testament describes, which is hands-on, relational prayer. Brown's studies measured that practice, and she called for larger replications.

Vineyard and other practitioners have increasingly taught consent, dignity and listening before praying. They emphasise that healing prayer is offered, not imposed, and that disabled believers are full members of Christ's body.

strawMen.strawMan: The mediating view does not really expect God to heal.
strawMen.correction: Its practitioners pray for the sick constantly and report many healings. They deny only that healing is guaranteed and that the unhealed are at fault.

strawMen.strawMan: Keener claims to have proved miracles scientifically.
strawMen.correction: Keener argues something more modest: that miracle claims are widespread and credible enough that they cannot be dismissed in principle, and that supernatural explanations deserve consideration.

positive: Normalised healing prayer in evangelical, Anglican and Catholic churches without the excesses of faith formulas.
Encouraged pastoral honesty about suffering and unanswered prayer.
Stimulated serious historical and empirical study of healing claims.
negative: Wimber-era conferences also produced hype and unverified claims of their own.
Critics on both sides see the view as unstable: either too cautious or still too credulous.

adherents: Vineyard churches worldwide
Catholic Charismatic Renewal and Christian Healing Ministries
Many charismatic Anglican and evangelical congregations
Continuationist biblical scholars and historians

positions.name: Critics: cessationist, empirical and theology-of-suffering objections
positions.summary:
The critics raise three distinct kinds of objection. Cessationists, following B. B. Warfield, hold that the miraculous gift of healing belonged to the apostolic age and authenticated new revelation. God still heals in answer to prayer, they say, but through providence, not through healers with a gift.

Empirical critics, both Christian and secular, insist that claims be verified. They point to investigations that found no verified cures, to exposed frauds, and to randomised trials that found no effect. Theologians of suffering such as Joni Eareckson Tada, who has lived with quadriplegia since 1967, argue that guaranteed-healing theology misreads Scripture and wounds the sick, and that God often works his deepest purposes through weakness.

Most Christian critics affirm that God can and does heal. Their objections are to the claim that healing is guaranteed, to the claim that gifted healers exist today, or to unverified claims.

figures.name: B. B. Warfield
figures.profession: Reformed theologian, Princeton Theological Seminary
figures.bio: Warfield's lectures, published as *Counterfeit Miracles* (1918), argued that the charismata were confined to the apostles and those on whom they laid hands, as credentials of revelation. He critiqued patristic, medieval Catholic, Irvingite, faith-cure and Christian Science miracle claims. His work remains the classic statement of Protestant cessationism.

figures.name: William A. Nolen
figures.profession: Surgeon and author, Minnesota
figures.bio: Nolen attended a Kathryn Kuhlman service and followed up on people who had claimed healing there. In his book he reported that he found no case of cure of organic disease. He found psychosomatic relief, and some tragic outcomes, including a woman with spinal cancer who discarded her brace and suffered collapse of a vertebra. He also investigated Filipino 'psychic surgeons'.

works.title: Healing: A Doctor in Search of a Miracle

figures.name: Joni Eareckson Tada
figures.profession: Author, artist, founder of Joni and Friends
figures.bio: Tada became quadriplegic in a 1967 diving accident and later lived with chronic pain and cancer. She sought healing early on, including at healing services, and over decades she has written about God's sovereign purposes in suffering. She affirms that God can heal, rejects guaranteed-healing teaching, and has built a global disability ministry.

works.title: When God Weeps

figures.name: Hank Hanegraaff
figures.profession: Christian apologist, radio host
figures.bio: Hanegraaff's books criticised Word of Faith healing teaching and the 1990s 'laughing revival' phenomena. He argued that faith formulas blame the sick and that many reported healings are unverified or psychosomatic.

figures.name: James Randi
figures.profession: Stage magician and sceptical investigator
figures.bio: Randi, a secular sceptic, investigated several televangelist healers. In 1986 he publicly exposed Peter Popoff's use of a hidden earpiece through which his wife fed him details about audience members, which Popoff presented as divine revelation. Randi's work is often cited by Christian critics of fraudulent healing ministries.

positions.context:
Protestant scepticism toward post-apostolic miracles goes back to the Reformation polemic against Catholic relics and shrines. It was systematised by Warfield in response to the faith-cure movement and Christian Science. In the twentieth century it was joined by medical scepticism, which grew as scientific medicine became more effective, and by the exposure of fraud in televangelism during the 1980s.

In the late twentieth century evangelical reflection on suffering, by Tada, C. S. Lewis and D. A. Carson among others, offered a pastoral rather than polemical critique. Empirical research also matured. Asser and Swan's 1998 paediatrics study documented preventable child deaths in faith-healing families, and the 2006 STEP trial tested distant intercessory prayer.
claims: God can and does heal in answer to prayer, but healing is not guaranteed in this life.
Cessationists hold that the gift of healing, as practised by the apostles, authenticated revelation and ceased. Healing today comes through providence and prayer, not gifted healers.
The atonement secures bodily healing finally at the resurrection, not on demand now.
Suffering, including illness and disability, can be the setting of God's deepest work, and the sick must never be blamed for lack of faith.
Healing claims should be medically verified, and the record includes many unverified, temporary, psychosomatic and fraudulent claims.
Overclaiming causes real harm: guilt, financial exploitation and avoidable deaths.

scriptures.reading: Paul prayed three times for removal of his thorn and was refused. God's strength is perfected in weakness.
Signs, wonders and mighty deeds were 'the signs of an apostle', marks of a unique office.
God bore witness to the apostolic message with signs and wonders. Miracles confirmed the first preaching of the gospel.
Paul recommends wine for Timothy's stomach and frequent illnesses. This is ordinary remedy, not a healing gift.
Our light affliction works a far more exceeding weight of glory. Suffering serves eternal purposes.
Present sufferings are not worth comparing to future glory. Creation and believers groan until the body's redemption.
The man's blindness was not due to his sin or his parents'. Illness is not a verdict on faith.
False christs and false prophets will show great signs and wonders. Miracles do not validate themselves.
God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more pain. Final healing belongs to the new creation.

arguments.text: Paul himself, who healed others, could not heal Trophimus or remove his own thorn, and recommended remedies for Timothy. Healing was never at the disposal of faith even in the apostolic circle.
Hebrews describes miracles as God's confirmation of the apostolic message in the past tense, consistent with their role as credentials of revelation.

Investigations have repeatedly found no verified cures of organic disease where healings were loudly claimed. Examples include Nolen's follow-up of Kuhlman cases and the exposure of Popoff's earpiece in 1986.
Asser and Swan's 1998 study in *Pediatrics* examined 172 child deaths in faith-healing families and judged that most children would likely have survived with medical treatment.

The 2006 STEP trial, involving about 1,800 cardiac bypass patients, found that distant intercessory prayer had no effect on recovery. Those who knew they were prayed for had somewhat more complications.
If healing is guaranteed to faith, the unhealed must lack faith. Since faithful saints in Scripture and history died of illness, the premise must be false.

critiques.text: Warfield's cessationism depends on Enlightenment assumptions about testimony and on a reading of 'signs of an apostle' that Scripture does not require. Healing gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 are given to ordinary believers.
Critics build a theology around unanswered prayer and treat sickness as God's tool. Jesus treated sickness as an enemy, never as a blessing in disguise.

critiques.from: Candy Gunther Brown and other researchers
critiques.text: Distant-prayer trials like STEP do not test the hands-on, relational prayer practised in healing ministries. Field studies of that practice have produced different results that deserve replication.
Western sceptics underweight testimony from the Global South, where healing claims are pervasive and sometimes medically documented.

responses.text: Cessationists answer that the gifts in 1 Corinthians 12 belonged to the apostolic churches. They argue that ecclesiastical history after the apostles shows a marked decline in such gifts, as even some Fathers acknowledged.
Tada and others affirm that sickness is an enemy and a consequence of the fall, but hold that God, who is sovereign over enemies, can use even them for good, as he used the cross.
Critics accept that STEP tested a different practice. They note that the Mozambique study was small and uncontrolled, which leaves suggestion and expectancy as possible explanations.
Many critics agree that testimony matters and should be heard. Their point is that all claims, from anywhere, should be documented and evaluated by the same standards.

strawMen.strawMan: Critics of the healing movement do not believe God heals.
strawMen.correction: Most Christian critics, including Warfield and Tada, affirm that God heals in answer to prayer. They dispute the means, the guarantees or the specific claims.

strawMen.strawMan: Theologians of suffering think sickness is good.
strawMen.correction: Tada and others call sickness an evil and a result of the fall. They argue that God redeems suffering, not that he delights in it.

strawMen.strawMan: Cessationists say Christians should not pray for the sick.
strawMen.correction: Cessationists encourage prayer for the sick, as James 5 directs. They deny that individuals today possess a miraculous gift of healing.

positive: Protected vulnerable people from fraud and from abandoning medical care.
Gave suffering believers a theology that dignifies them instead of blaming them.
Encouraged honesty and verification in healing claims.
negative: Cessationist polemic has at times dismissed genuine Christian experience wholesale.
A theology of suffering, wrongly applied, can drift into passivity toward illness or reluctance to pray boldly.

Medical researchers and sceptical investigators (including non-Christians)

The atonement is the ground of all healing, partly tasted now and fully received at the resurrection.

Matthew applies Isaiah 53 to physical healing, which proves that healing is in the atonement.
Jesus' healings fulfil Isaiah as signs that the kingdom has arrived, a pattern the church continues in part.
Matthew sees Isaiah fulfilled in Jesus' earthly ministry. That does not make healing a present guarantee for every believer.
A standing promise: the prayer of faith will heal the sick.
A normal church practice of expectant prayer, set within God's sovereign will.

Consistent with the New Testament pattern, though most scholars treat the longer ending of Mark as a later addition, so it is not used as the main foundation.
Absent from the earliest manuscripts, and in any case the signs are tied to confirming the apostles' preaching (v. 20).

title: Hearing God's voice: guidance, impressions and the sufficiency of Scripture
question: Does God speak to believers today beyond Scripture, through an inner voice, impressions, dreams or prophetic words, and how should Christians seek guidance for their decisions?
intro:
Since the 1980s a widespread evangelical and charismatic emphasis has taught that believers can and should learn to 'hear God's voice' in a personal, conversational way. Dallas Willard's *Hearing God* (1999, revised from *In Search of Guidance*, 1984) gave the idea philosophical and pastoral depth. Mark Virkler's 'four keys' and two-way journaling offered a practical method. Jack Deere, a former Dallas Seminary professor, argued from Scripture and church history that God still speaks in many ways.

Reformed theologians raise concerns rooted in the sufficiency of Scripture (2 Timothy 3:16-17). The Westminster Confession (1.6) holds that nothing is to be added to Scripture 'by new revelations of the Spirit', and Calvin and Luther both opposed 'enthusiasts' who claimed private revelations. Kevin DeYoung's *Just Do Something* (2009) argues that anxious searching for God's specific will leads to paralysis. A related but distinct 'wisdom model', set out in Garry Friesen's *Decision Making and the Will of God* (1980), holds that God has no hidden 'individual will' that believers must discover. Within his revealed moral will, they are free to choose wisely.

The three positions agree that Scripture is supreme. They disagree on whether God ordinarily gives personal, extra-biblical communication, and on how decisions should be made.

positions.name: Conversational relationship: God still speaks personally
positions.summary:
This view holds that God's purpose is a conversational relationship with his people, not only rules to follow. As Willard puts it, believers are meant to live in an ongoing friendship with God, in which he speaks and they learn to recognise his voice. God speaks above all through Scripture. He also speaks through the 'still small voice' of inner impressions, through dreams and visions, through other people, through circumstances and through prophecy.

These communications never add to Scripture's doctrine and must always be tested by it. They concern application, such as encouragement, direction and conviction, not new truths about God. Learning to recognise God's voice is described as a skill developed over time, like Samuel learning to distinguish it. Willard stresses character and union with God more than decision-making technique. Virkler offers a structured method of quieting, picturing, attending to spontaneous thoughts and journaling. Deere argues that Scripture and church history, including Reformation and Puritan figures, show God speaking this way.

figures.name: Dallas Willard
figures.profession: Philosopher, University of Southern California; writer on spiritual formation
figures.bio: Willard was a respected phenomenologist who wrote widely read books on discipleship and spiritual formation. *Hearing God* treats God's speaking as part of a 'conversational relationship' grounded in the reality of God's kingdom. It also warns against using God's voice to avoid responsibility, and it insists that God's 'voice' is recognised by its quality, its spirit and its content, and above all by its harmony with Scripture.

Believers recognise God's voice as spontaneous thoughts that 'light upon' the mind, quiet themselves, look for vision, and write down the dialogue in a journal. His courses have been widely used in charismatic churches.

figures.name: A. W. Tozer
figures.profession: Christian and Missionary Alliance pastor and editor
figures.bio: Tozer's devotional classic, *The Pursuit of God*, includes a chapter on 'the speaking voice'. In it he argues that God is by nature continuously speaking and that the Bible is the written expression of that living voice, to be heard personally, not merely studied. Later writers on hearing God often cite him as a forerunner, though his own emphasis was on hearing God through Scripture.

figures.name: Priscilla Shirer
figures.profession: Bible teacher and author
figures.bio: Shirer's study on discerning God's voice became popular in evangelical women's ministry and beyond. It presents the Holy Spirit's personal guidance as normal for believers, always tested by Scripture and recognised by its character.

positions.context:
The modern emphasis has several sources. One is the charismatic renewal's expectation of spiritual gifts. Another is evangelical interest in spiritual formation, through Willard, Richard Foster's *Celebration of Discipline* (1978) and the rediscovery of practices such as Ignatian discernment and Brother Lawrence's 'practice of the presence of God'. A third is the wide influence of devotional writing like Tozer's. Within Southern Baptist life, Henry Blackaby's *Experiencing God* (1990) popularised the idea that God speaks through the Bible, prayer, circumstances and the church.

In practice the movement ranges from Willard's careful, Scripture-bounded account to more expansive charismatic methods. Popular evangelical language ('God laid it on my heart', 'I felt led') shows how deeply the expectation has spread.
claims: God's goal is a personal, conversational relationship with his children, not merely rule-keeping.
God speaks primarily through Scripture, but also through inner impressions, dreams, visions, other believers, circumstances and prophecy.
Such communication never adds doctrine to Scripture and is always subject to it.
Recognising God's voice is a skill learned over time, through Scripture, prayer, community and experience.
God's voice is recognised by its consistency with Scripture and Christ's character, by its peace and authority, and by its fruit.
Treating God as speaking only through the text risks reducing the relationship to study and making the Spirit's present work invisible.

scriptures.reading: 'My sheep hear my voice.' Hearing Christ is a normal mark of belonging to him.
Samuel had to learn to recognise the Lord's voice with Eli's help. Hearing God is a learned discernment.
God spoke to Elijah not in wind, earthquake or fire but in a 'still small voice', an inner, quiet communication.
The Spirit told Philip to approach the chariot, giving specific personal direction for ministry.
The Spirit spoke to Peter about the men at the door, an example of specific guidance in real time.
The Spirit forbade Paul to preach in Asia, and a night vision called him to Macedonia. Guidance in the New Testament included impressions and dreams.
The prophet stood to watch and see what God would say, and was told to write the vision. Virkler's model of quieting, looking and journaling draws on this.
Those led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God. Being led is normal Christian experience.
'Thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way.' God promises guidance to his people.

arguments.text: Throughout Scripture, God's people receive personal communication. In Acts this includes ordinary believers such as Ananias, Philip and Cornelius, not only apostles. Nothing in the New Testament says this pattern would end.
Jesus describes his followers as sheep who know his voice. A relationship in which one party never speaks personally would not be the friendship Jesus offers.
Willard argues that a personal God who indwells believers would naturally communicate personally. Denying this makes the Christian life functionally deistic, with God present only in a book.

Christian tradition has long practised discernment of God's personal leading: Augustine's 'take up and read' (*Confessions* 8.12), Ignatius of Loyola's rules for the discernment of spirits, Quaker attention to the inner light, and Puritan reflection on providential 'impressions'.

Deere notes that Scottish Reformation and Covenanter figures such as George Wishart, John Knox and Samuel Rutherford were credited by contemporaries with prophetic foresight. The Reformed tradition's own history is therefore more open to God's present speaking than its confessional cessationism suggests.

The Westminster Confession speaks of the 'whole counsel of God' for doctrine, worship and salvation. Personal guidance about which job to take or whom to visit does not add to that counsel, so it does not violate sufficiency.

critiques.text: Scripture is sufficient for all of faith and life, and nothing is to be added to it by new revelations of the Spirit. Expecting regular personal communication tends to relativise Scripture and opens the door to the private claims the Reformers called fanaticism.
The search for God's voice on every decision produces anxiety, passivity and paralysis. It also becomes a way to avoid responsibility, because 'God told me' ends discussion and cannot be challenged.

critiques.from: Garry Friesen and the wisdom model
critiques.text: The idea that God has a detailed 'individual will' to be discovered through inner impressions is not taught in Scripture. Impressions are subjective, cannot be verified, and are easily confused with our own desires.

Treating spontaneous thoughts as God's voice and journaling them as dialogue blurs the line between imagination and revelation. It gives believers no reliable way to tell their own subconscious from God.
Claims of 'God told me', about marriage partners, business ventures or church decisions, have often caused harm and spiritual manipulation when they proved wrong.

responses.text: Willard and Deere agree that nothing may be added to Scripture's doctrine. They argue that personal guidance is application, not new doctrine, and that the Confession itself (1.6) acknowledges the necessity of the Spirit's inward illumination and leaves many circumstances to 'Christian prudence'.

Willard explicitly warned against seeking a word for every decision. He taught that mature believers often decide by wisdom, and that God's speaking aims at character and partnership, not at relieving us of responsibility.

Proponents acknowledge that impressions are fallible. That is why they insist on testing by Scripture, by mature counsel, by fruit and over time. Fallibility calls for discernment, not for denying that God speaks.

Virkler insists that journaled words must be submitted to Scripture and to spiritual counsellors. He argues that God sanctifies the imagination rather than bypassing it, as in the visions of the prophets.
Proponents agree that 'God told me' should not be used to control others. Willard specifically criticised that use as a sign of immaturity.

strawMen.strawMan: People who 'hear God' think their impressions are equal to Scripture.
strawMen.correction: Willard, Deere and Virkler all teach that Scripture is the final authority and that impressions must be tested by it. The debate is about whether such impressions exist and how much weight they carry.

strawMen.strawMan: Hearing God means believers expect an audible voice.
strawMen.correction: Most proponents describe God's speaking as inner thoughts, impressions or a sense of conviction, and occasionally dreams. They do not normally mean an audible voice.

strawMen.strawMan: This view is a purely charismatic innovation.
strawMen.correction: Willard was not a typical charismatic, and the practice of personal discernment draws on Catholic, Quaker, Puritan and evangelical devotional traditions.

positive: Nurtured a warm, relational prayer life and attentiveness to God for many believers.
Brought spiritual formation practices into evangelical churches.
Encouraged believers to expect God's presence in everyday life.
negative: Popular forms can foster 'God told me' manipulation and decisions later regretted.
Some believers report anxiety and guilt when they do not 'hear' anything.
Can shift attention from Scripture's clear commands to the search for private words.

adherents: Charismatic and Pentecostal churches
Many evangelicals shaped by spiritual formation (Willard, Foster) and by *Experiencing God*
Vineyard and Reformed-charismatic congregations
Catholic and Anglican practitioners of discernment
